blocks.title: Stages of compilation
blocks.md: **Lexical analysis** splits the source code into **tokens** (keywords, identifiers, numbers, operators) and removes spaces and comments. **Syntax analysis** (parsing) checks the tokens against the grammar and builds a **syntax tree**. **Semantic analysis** checks meaning (for example, types). **Code generation** produces machine or intermediate code. **Optimisation** makes the code faster or smaller.

blocks.title: Translators and tools
blocks.md: A **compiler** translates the whole source program to an executable (fast run, errors reported together). An **interpreter** translates and runs line by line (easy testing, slower run, source needed at run time). An **assembler** translates assembly. A **linker** combines object files and libraries into one executable; a **loader** places it in memory to run. Some languages compile to **bytecode** that a virtual machine interprets.

blocks.title: Types of error
blocks.md: **Syntax error**: breaks the grammar (a missing bracket); found at translation. **Logic error**: the program runs but gives wrong results (using + instead of -); found by testing. **Runtime error**: occurs while running (division by zero).

blocks.title: BNF
blocks.md: **Backus-Naur Form** defines a language's syntax with rules: <digit> ::= 0 | 1 | 2 | ... | 9 and <number> ::= <digit> | <digit><number>. The symbol | means 'or'; ::= means 'is defined as'. A string is valid if it can be built from the rules. Example: 305 is a valid <number> (digit, then digit, then digit).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The compiler finds syntax errors, not logic errors.
- Compiled code runs without the compiler; interpreted code needs the interpreter.
- BNF rules can be recursive; a rule that never ends in a base case is invalid.
